record.paper_title: Nuclei of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs - Central engine & conditions of star formation: Workshop summary and open questions
record.original_question: Do active galactic nuclei that genuinely lack a broad-line region exist, or are observed cases without broad emission lines mainly caused by observational biases such as spatial resolution and sensitivity, by obscuration and orientation effects, or by transient partial obscuration?

evidence.quote: 6. Do non-hidden broad line region AGN exist or is the lack of broad lines in these objects a matter of observational biases (e.g., spatial resolution, sensitivity)?
The existence of AGN without a broad line region has been hypothesized in the last decade.

There are objects in which we do not see broad lines due to obscuration/orientation effects. But objects with lower accretion rates might switch to different accretion mechanisms and do not possess a BLR. Such AGN have been observed.
My opinion is that objects actually lacking a BLR exist [...]

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An active galactic nucleus (AGN) is the compact, highly luminous central region of a galaxy powered by accretion onto a supermassive black hole. AGN spectra typically display broad permitted emission lines (with widths of order 10^3–10^4 km/s) attributed to a "broad-line region" (BLR) of dense gas clouds orbiting close to the black hole. Some AGN show only narrow emission lines in their direct optical spectra. Such cases can arise because (i) the BLR is present but hidden from direct view by obscuring dusty material or specific orientation (e.g. a dusty torus seen edge-on, sometimes revealed via polarized light), (ii) variable or partial obscuration transiently suppresses the broad lines, or (iii) limited spatial resolution and sensitivity prevent the detection of an intrinsically faint BLR. Alternatively, it has been hypothesized that at sufficiently low accretion rates (e.g. radiatively inefficient accretion flows) the physical conditions required to sustain a BLR are no longer met, so the BLR is genuinely absent ("true type-2" or "non-hidden BLR" AGN).

Question: Do AGN that intrinsically lack a broad-line region exist as a real physical class, or can every observed AGN without broad emission lines be accounted for by observational biases (such as insufficient spatial resolution or sensitivity), by obscuration and orientation effects, or by transient partial obscuration? Equivalently: determine whether there is a genuine population of AGN in which the BLR is physically absent rather than merely hidden, and characterize the accretion regime (e.g. Eddington ratio threshold) in which such absence occurs.
artifact.status_search_result: The existence of "true type-2" AGN that intrinsically lack a BLR remains an open question. Theoretical work (e.g. disk-wind models) predicts BLR disappearance below a critical luminosity / Eddington ratio (typically below ~1%), and several candidate sources have been reported, including a 2025 candidate identified via a central tidal disruption event in SDSS J233454.07+145712.9. However, the literature still describes the existence of true type-2 AGN as not definitively established, with many candidates still potentially explainable by obscuration, orientation, or sensitivity limitations.

status_evidence.title: Disc outflows and high-luminosity true type 2 AGN (MNRAS, 2016)
status_evidence.snippet: Disk-wind mass conservation implies that the minimal column required by an observable BLR cannot be sustained below a certain luminosity; transition to 'true' type 2 AGN occurs in the regime of radiatively inefficient accretion.
status_evidence.claim: Theoretical predictions support the physical existence of true type-2 AGN at low accretion rates.

status_evidence.title: A candidate for True Type-2 AGN without hidden central BLRs Identified by central Tidal Disruption Event (arXiv:2505.20821)
status_evidence.snippet: SDSS J233454.07+145712.9 shows power-law continuum and AGN activity but no broad emission lines, indicating a candidate TT2AGN without hidden central BLRs; the extreme existence of True Type-2 AGN is still an open question.
status_evidence.claim: Recent candidates exist, but the question of whether genuine non-hidden-BLR AGN exist is still open.

status_evidence.title: On the Disappearance of the Broad-Line Region in Low-Luminosity AGN (ApJL)
status_evidence.snippet: Argues for disappearance of the BLR below a critical luminosity in low-luminosity AGN.
status_evidence.claim: Supports the hypothesis of intrinsic BLR absence at low luminosities.
